blocks.raw: <Tip>ASD = working stress = elastic = simple. LRFD = factored loads = factored capacity = sophisticated. In ASD, the designer prevents yielding. In LRFD, the designer permits (and expects) yielding but ensures it is controlled and ductile. Load factors > 1 (amplify); resistance factors < 1 (reduce). The product (load factor × resistance factor) is the effective safety margin.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing ASD and LRFD by mixing checks. ASD uses unfactored loads and allowable stresses: f ≤ Fa. LRFD uses factored loads and factored capacities: Pu ≤ φPn. Never mix unfactored loads with φ factors or vice versa; the result is unsafe.","Assuming LRFD always gives a lower design (more economical). LRFD often designs more conservatively than ASD in certain regions because factored demands amplify uncertainty. The two methods are not strictly comparable on cost; they address different uncertainties.","Forgetting the difference between load factors for LRFD: U = 1.2D + 1.6L (modern) vs. U = 1.4DL + 1.7LL (older). Always check which code edition applies. Using the wrong factors gives incorrect demand calculations.","Treating φ factors as uniform. φ = 0.90 for flexure (ductile) but φ = 0.70 for tied columns and bearing (brittle). The difference reflects failure mode control. Applying the same φ to all limit states is incorrect.","Assuming ASD allows unlimited stress. ASD limits stress to fractions of Fy (0.60Fy, 0.66Fy, 0.40Fy), not Fy itself. The material must remain in the elastic region. Exceeding the allowable stress is failure, just as exceeding Pu ≤ φPn is failure in LRFD.","Missing the point that both methods aim for safety; they differ only in how safety is introduced. ASD is deterministic (work stress < yield); LRFD is probabilistic (factors reflect uncertainty). Neither is 'safer' in absolute terms; they are calibrated to similar reliability indices."] />
